1.goal: To name the scene before any audio: two people on the buyer's side talking to each other, and him on the line, silent.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask when this last happened to him for real. One answer, then move.
Say out loud that this is the skill he named as the one that would fix the others. The product today is not understanding — it is what he does in the second he does not understand.
exact: You told me this is the one skill that would fix the others. Today is not about understanding all of it — it is about what you do in the second you do not.
1.expected: One concrete call, most likely one of his own.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about a call in Portuguese where two other people ran ahead of him.
1.challenge: Ask what he did at the moment he lost the thread, and whether it worked.
1.monitoring: Whether he frames the problem as vocabulary or as speed. Today's answer is neither: it is the repair.
1.evidence: The example he gives — it is the scene the lesson gives back.
1.transition: Move on when he has given one concrete example.

2.goal: Who the two are, and why he is listening before speaking.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the card on screen together.
run: Give him time to read.
Confirm out loud: they have already looked at other companies, and the call starts before he joins.
2.expected: That the two are deciding what to ask him, not asking him anything yet.
2.support: If the roles blur, ask which of the two will still be in the room when the decision is made.
2.challenge: Ask what he would want to hear them say before he speaks.
2.monitoring: Do not anticipate anything about the content. The prediction is the next stage and it lives on him not knowing.
2.evidence: Whether he can say what the two are deciding.
2.transition: Move on when he says what these two people are deciding.

3.goal: To risk what is coming, before hearing it.
3.interaction: T–S, one prediction, then one listening.
run: Read the line on screen out loud and ask the question.
Accept ANY guess; do not confirm and do not correct.
Then play the first turn ONCE.
exact: The two options, if he will not commit: “What impressed him, or what worries him?”
3.expected: Either answer is fine. What you want is that he commits before hearing.
3.support: If he will not commit, offer the two options and let him choose one.
3.challenge: Ask what the first six words would be in each case.
3.monitoring: If you confirm the guess, he stops risking on the next ones.
3.evidence: Whether he risks a hypothesis at all.
3.transition: Move on when he has risked a guess and heard it once.

4.goal: One whole listening, no transcript, only for the two questions on screen.
4.interaction: S listens to the ninety seconds straight through, then T–S.
run: Play the ninety seconds in one go, with no pause.
The questions are already on screen — read them WITH him before you press play.
exact: Did they ask him for anything in this call? (No. They decided what they are going to ask for.)
4.support: If he asks for the transcript, hold it until stage 5. The difficulty here is part of the task.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two speakers he found harder to follow, and why.
4.monitoring: Whether he listens for the decision or for the numbers. The decision is what the call is about.
4.evidence: What one listening gives him without support. It is the first listening measure of the cycle.
4.transition: Move on when he answers both, even partially.

5.goal: To separate what was said from what was only implied — and to find what is not there.
5.interaction: S classifies; you check and stop the audio where he lost it.
run: Play again, stopping at the points where he loses it.
He classifies; you check.
exact: What does a “no” about delivering in English change? (Price and timeline.) Does it change whether they do it? (No.)
5.expected: One of the six was not in the call, and finding it is the point.
5.support: If an item resists, replay only the ten seconds it depends on.
5.challenge: Ask what they WOULD have said if a “no” did end the deal.
5.monitoring: The item that decides: “a no would end the deal” is NOT in the call. It is the comfortable reading — and it is the opposite of what was said.
5.evidence: Whether he catches the limit case on his own.
5.transition: Move on when he gets the limit case right.

6.goal: For HIM to formulate what separates a repair that works from one that does not. Do not hand him the rule.
6.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S until he words it himself.
run: Four lines on screen; he marks the two that recover what was missed.
Then ask what the two he marked have in common.
If he says interrupting is rude, answer once and move on: on a call, the person who asks is the person who is following.
exact: What do the two you marked have in common?
6.expected: The answer you want, from him: the two say WHICH piece was missed. The others hand the choice back to the other person, who then repeats whatever THEY think mattered.
6.support: If the difference will not come, read one of each out loud and ask which one tells the other person where to restart.
6.challenge: Ask him to turn one of the weak repairs into a strong one, on the spot.
6.monitoring: Whether he reaches the distinction himself, and whether politeness is what is blocking it.
6.evidence: His own wording of the difference. It is what stage 7 practices.
6.transition: Move on when he has said the difference in his own words.

7.goal: The five repairs said out loud, at the right moment.
7.interaction: T plays and stops; S repairs on the spot. Four stopping points.
run: Play again and stop at the four marked points. At each one he produces the repair, on the spot.
If he waits for the end, go back and redo the point — waiting for the end is exactly the behavior this lesson exists to replace.
Correction here is immediate and dry. At stage 8 there is no correcting.
7.expected: Four repairs, each naming which piece was missed.
7.support: If the repair will not come, give the first three words and let him finish.
7.challenge: Stop at a fifth point he did not expect and see whether the repair still comes.
7.monitoring: Whether the repair arrives at the moment of the loss, or after the speaker finishes.
7.evidence: How many of the four come out at the right moment.
7.transition: Move on when the four repairs have come out, however rough.

8.goal: The production of the lesson — he joins a call that is already running and nobody stops for him.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Diane, speaking fast, and you do not invite him in.
run: The call is already running when he joins. Speak fast on purpose, once, with a number in the middle. He has to ask for it back.
HE HAS TO COME IN UNINVITED. Do not ask “Caio, what do you think?” — that question does the work that is his.
Do not correct during. Note it and hand it back at stage 9.
Record it. It is the first interaction measure of the cycle.
8.expected: At least one repair and one confirmation, both produced without being invited.
8.support: If he does not come in at all, keep going and let the silence stand. The absence is the evidence.
8.challenge: Give a second number, faster, and see whether the second repair is quicker than the first.
8.monitoring: Whether he comes in without being invited, and whether the repair names the piece.
8.evidence: The recording, and how many repairs he made. Both go in the record.
8.transition: Move on when he has asked one question and confirmed one piece of information, or at four minutes.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for one repair at a higher speed.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the board together, then one replay at 1.25x.
run: Two things, no more — one that worked and one that did not come out. Straight, without softening.
Count the repairs out loud with him. He asked for evidence of progress; four repairs on a call he could not follow IS evidence that he can hold it.
Then: same passage at 1.25x, ONE repair allowed. He chooses which — and the choice says what he considers essential.
Do not add new content. It is the same task under one changed constraint.
exact: Same passage, a quarter faster — and you get to stop me once. Which one do you spend it on?
9.expected: One repair, spent on the piece that carries the decision rather than on the first thing missed.
9.support: If he spends it on the first gap, ask afterwards which piece he would rather have had.
9.challenge: Run it once more at 1.5x with the same single repair.
9.monitoring: Which repair he chooses. It says what he treats as essential under pressure.
9.evidence: The number of repairs in round one, and which one he spent in round two.
9.transition: Move on when the faster round has been done.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close.
run: He ticks what he recognizes. Do not argue with the marks.

Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has the same call at full speed and with no transcript, and two podcasts where the interviewer repairs constantly — and nobody hears it as failure.
Announce lesson 3: grammar, and the object is the error he named himself — she like, he have.
exact: Next lesson is grammar, and it is the one you named yourself: she like, he have. You already hear it — next time you fix it.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, ask which repair he would use on the next call he is already booked for.
10.challenge: Ask when the next English call is, and which repair he takes into it.
10.monitoring: A low mark after four repairs that worked is worth recording — it is the gap between doing and knowing that he did.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. Lesson 2 of the four in the block; lesson 4 reads them together.
